Vishnusharman.description: The narrator and teacher who tells the story to the princes.

Jewel.description: A merchant in the city of Trumpet-Flower who loses his fortune and encounters a Jain monk in a dream.

barber.description: A barber who, after witnessing Jewel's fortune, tries to replicate his success with disastrous results.

Jain monk.description: A monk who appears in Jewel's dream and later in reality, turning into gold when struck.

abbot.description: The head of the Jain monastery whom the barber approaches with his request.

princes.description: The audience to whom Vishnusharman narrates the story.

Book V.description: The fifth book of the Panchatantra, titled 'Ill-considered Action.'

Trumpet-Flower.description: A city in the southern country where the story takes place.

Jain.description: Refers to Jainism, an ancient Indian religion emphasizing non-violence and asceticism.

Brahmans.description: Brahmans are members of the priestly caste in Hindu society, often associated with religious rituals and scholarship; the term 'Brahman' is also used generically for an individual member.

decree of fate.description: A phrase referring to destiny or predetermined events.

salvation.description: Spiritual liberation or deliverance, often used in Indian religious contexts.

despondency.description: A state of low spirits or hopelessness.

self-starvation.description: The act of intentionally refusing to eat, often as a form of suicide or ascetic practice.

manicure.description: To trim, clean, and care for the nails, especially of the hands.

obeisance.description: A gesture expressing respect or submission, such as a bow.

benediction.description: A blessing, especially one given by a religious figure.

celibacy.description: The state of abstaining from marriage and sexual relations, often for religious reasons.

neophyte.description: A new convert or novice, especially in a religious context.

cudgels.description: Short, thick sticks used as weapons.

acacia wood.description: Wood from the acacia tree, commonly used in India.

citadel.description: A fortress protecting a city, often the strongest part of the city.

summonser.description: An official who delivers a summons or legal notice.

impaled.description: Executed by being pierced with a sharp stake, a form of capital punishment.

Godly.description: A Brahman living in a certain town, husband to the mother and father of the baby boy, who raises a mongoose alongside his son.

mungoose.description: A pet mongoose raised alongside the Brahman's son, ultimately killed by the mother after saving the child.

black snake.description: A venomous serpent that threatens the Brahman's baby and is killed by the mungoose.

salves.description: Ointments used to promote healing of the skin or as protection.

gruel.description: A thin liquid food of oatmeal or other meal boiled in milk or water.

benefactor.description: One who does good or provides help, especially by giving money or assistance.

lamenting.description: Expressing grief or sorrow, often in a demonstrative way.

Terror-Joy.description: A master-magician whom the Brahmans meet on their journey; he provides them with magic quills.

Shiva.description: The great god worshipped by the Brahmans during their travels.

King Vinavatsa.description: The king mentioned as reigning at the time of the events.

Rama.description: A legendary king referenced in the story, indicating a time long past.

Avanti.description: A historical region in ancient India, visited by the Brahmans.

Sipra.description: A river in the Avanti country where the Brahmans bathe.

Himalaya Mountains.description: The famous mountain range in northern India, where the Brahmans are instructed to go.

Vishnu.description: A major Hindu deity, mentioned in a proverb about effort and fate.

flunkeyism.description: Obsequious behavior, especially as a servant in a royal court.

pawnshop.description: A place where personal items are left as security for a loan.

usury.description: The practice of lending money at unreasonably high interest rates.

capitalist.description: A person who invests capital, especially in business ventures.

magician.description: A person who practices magic or sorcery.

quill.description: A feather used as a writing instrument or, in this context, a magical object.

decrepitude.description: The state of being worn out or weakened by old age.

subaqueous.description: Existing, formed, or taking place underwater.

lion.description: A dead lion whose bones are found in the forest and is brought back to life by the Brahmans' scholarship.

man of sense.description: The fourth Brahman, who lacks scholarship but possesses practical wisdom and survives by his prudence.

wheel-bearer.description: A character who listens to the story and argues that fate, not sense, determines survival.

gold-finder.description: A character who asks the wheel-bearer to explain his reasoning.

scholarship.description: In this context, refers to learned knowledge or academic attainment, especially in religious or classical studies.

dullard.description: An archaic English term meaning a slow or stupid person.

nullity.description: An archaic term meaning nothingness or the state of being null.

stanza.description: A grouped set of lines in a poem, often set off from others by a blank line or indentation.

Hundred-Wit.description: A fish living in the pond, known for his intelligence and resourcefulness.

Thousand-Wit.description: Another fish, considered even more clever than Hundred-Wit, confident in his ability to escape danger.

Single-Wit.description: A frog who is friends with the two fishes, cautious and guided by simple wisdom.

Death.description: A personified force and its agents symbolizing inevitable fate and the end of life.

cistern.description: A water storage tank or reservoir, often used in Indian settings for storing water.

inclosed.description: An archaic spelling of 'enclosed', meaning surrounded or shut in.

padling.description: An archaic or variant spelling of 'paddling', meaning moving through water with short movements.

dissuasion.description: The act of advising against something; discouragement.

Prig.description: A donkey who carries laundry by day and roams freely at night; he is egotistical and wishes to sing.

jackal.description: A cunning animal who befriends Prig and tries to dissuade him from singing while stealing cucumbers.

comestible.description: An archaic term meaning something edible or fit to be eaten.

provender.description: An old-fashioned word for food or fodder, especially for livestock.

conch-shell.description: A large spiral shell from the Indian Ocean, often used as a musical instrument in Indian culture.

hobbled.description: To tie an animal's legs together to restrict movement; here, refers to the donkey being restrained.

mortar.description: A heavy bowl used for grinding substances; in the story, it is fastened to the donkey's neck as punishment.

Slow.description: A weaver living in a certain town whose search for wood leads to an encounter with a fairy and a wish for extra limbs.

fairy.description: A supernatural being residing in the sissoo tree who offers to grant Slow a wish if he spares the tree.

wife.description: The weaver's spouse who counsels him to ask for extra arms and a head instead of a kingdom.

sissoo.description: A type of tree native to the Indian subcontinent, also known as Dalbergia sissoo.

Moon-Lord.description: A poetic reference to the Hindu moon god, Chandra, often used in Indian literature.

loom.description: A device used for weaving cloth.

apparatus.description: Equipment or tools needed for a specific purpose, here referring to weaving tools.

entrenchment.description: A defensive military position, used here metaphorically for the difficulties of kingship.

duplicity.description: Deceitfulness or double-dealing, especially in the context of political affairs.

bard.description: A poet or singer, often one who composes and recites verses celebrating legendary events.

hermit.description: A person living in solitude, often for religious reasons.

fiend.description: An evil spirit or demon; used here to describe the weaver's frightening appearance after his wish is granted.

sage.description: A wise person, often referenced in ancient Indian literature as a source of proverbs or teachings.

Seedy.description: A Brahman who dreams of future riches and prosperity after acquiring some barley-meal, only to lose everything due to his daydreaming.

cot.description: A simple, light bed, often used in India.

barley-meal.description: Ground barley, used as a food staple.

dowry.description: Property or money brought by a bride to her husband upon marriage.

reverie.description: A state of being pleasantly lost in one's thoughts; a daydream.

Moon.description: A ruler in a certain city who keeps monkeys and a ram for his son's amusement.

chief of the monkeys.description: The wise leader of the monkey pack who warns his followers of danger and ultimately escapes the king's city.

ram.description: A member of the herd kept for the prince's amusement, known for his gluttony and causing trouble in the kitchen.

cooks.description: The kitchen staff who are frequently angered by the ram's behavior.

retinue.description: The king's attendants who accompany him and are devoured by the fiend.

Sunday.description: A day of the week, referenced as auspicious for bathing in the magical lake.

Twilight.description: Personified as a being who catches the monkey, possibly a metaphor for death or fate.

veterinary.description: Relating to the medical care of animals.

monkeys-fat.description: Fat derived from monkeys, prescribed in the story as a remedy for burns on horses.

halters.description: Straps or ropes used for leading or tying animals.

palanquin.description: A covered litter for one passenger, carried on poles by several bearers.

lakh.description: A unit in the Indian numbering system equal to one hundred thousand.

bosom.description: The chest or breast, often used to signify affection or closeness.

proverb.description: A short, well-known saying expressing a general truth.

palace-roofs.description: The roofs of palaces, referenced as places where the monkey is seen.

lotuses.description: Aquatic plants with large, showy flowers, significant in Indian culture.

lotus-stalk.description: The stem of a lotus plant, used by the monkey to drink water safely.

Fine-Army.description: A king who rules a certain city and is the father of Pearl.

Pearl.description: The daughter of King Fine-Army, renowned for her perfect beauty and protected by magic.

horse-thief.description: A thief who attempts to steal the fiend in horse form and ultimately escapes him.

monkey.description: A monkey living in the banyan tree who interacts with the fiend and the horse-thief.

banyan.description: A type of large, sacred fig tree native to India, under which part of the story takes place.

magic circle.description: A protective circle drawn for magical or ritualistic purposes, believed to ward off evil.

waywardness.description: The quality of being willful, unpredictable, or disobedient.

prudence.description: Cautiousness or wisdom in practical affairs.

fate’s decree.description: A phrase referring to destiny or the will of fate determining events.

Honey-Host.description: King of Honey-Town, father of the three-breasted princess.

chamberlain.description: A royal official who advises King Honey-Host regarding the fate of the three-breasted princess.

Honey-Town.description: A city in the north country where King Honey-Host rules.

divine.description: Relating to the gods or the sacred, often used in the context of religious law.

Cruel.description: A fiend living in the forest who forces a Brahman to carry him, bound by a vow not to touch the ground with unwashed feet.

blind man.description: A poor man who marries the three-breasted princess and later regains his sight.

three-breasted princess.description: The daughter of King Honey-Host born with a physical deformity believed to be a bad omen, who later marries a blind man.

lotus-heart.description: The soft, tender center of a lotus flower, used metaphorically to describe softness.

vow.description: A solemn promise or oath, often of religious significance.

hundred thousand gold-pieces.description: A large sum of money, indicating wealth or a reward.

belly-pot.description: An archaic phrase meaning the stomach or belly.

kettle.description: A metal pot used for cooking or boiling.

butter-milk.description: A fermented dairy product, commonly used in Indian cuisine.

fate.description: The development of events beyond a person's control, regarded as predetermined.
